chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Salim, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Kindi, from his father, who was the master of the water-pourer (mihdar) of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Jibril (peace be upon him) said: 'We do not enter a house in which there is a statue/image that is not trampled upon.' The hadith is shortened.

key_terms.تِمْثَالٌ: Statue or image (of a living being)
key_terms.مِطْهَرَةُ: The water-pourer (one who pours water for ablution)

ai.seo_question: What condition prevents angels from entering a house according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes a spiritual principle where the presence of upright statues (timsal) obstructs the descent of angels, a concept central to Shia jurisprudence regarding the permissibility of images in domestic spaces. It highlights the distinction between mere representation and the veneration or prominence of the image, as indicated by the condition 'unless it is trampled upon,' which implies that lowly or discarded images do not carry the same spiritual weight. This narration is frequently cited by scholars like al-Shaykh al-Mufid and al-Tusi to discuss the ruling on statues of living beings versus inanimate objects.
